intro: People can talk without words. A red sign with eight sides says stop. A heart says love. A pin shows your club. These pictures are called symbols. In this unit, you will learn to read them.

Long ago, groups used symbols and codes too. Builders used a square and compass. A group in Italy put seven steps on a floor. Freemasons wrote notes in the pigpen code. You will try these ideas yourself.
You will make a class symbol. You will write your name in a secret code. You will also learn which secrets are happy and which ones you always tell a trusted grown-up.
bigQuestion: How do pictures, codes and secret words help a group share ideas?

timeline.t: Find a symbol on a sign or a building and say what it means.
Look at old symbols: the seven-step floor and the square and compass.
Talk with your class about what you all love.
Draw a simple class symbol together.
Make a key that matches each letter to a sign.
Write your name in the pigpen code.
Make up a class password and a quiet hand signal.
Sort happy secrets from unsafe ones, and name your trusted grown-ups.

words.d: a picture or shape that stands for an idea
a board with a picture, shape or words that gives a message
a small sign you wear to show a group you belong to
a tool with two legs, used to draw circles
a way to swap letters for shapes, numbers or other signs
a list that shows which sign goes with which letter
a secret word that lets you in or shows you belong
an adult who listens to you and helps keep you safe

test.q: A red heart on a card stands for what idea?
test.why: A heart is a symbol for love, like the heart on Sam's card.

choices: A picture that stands for an idea
test.why: A symbol is a picture that stands for an idea.

test.q: How many steps are shown on the old floor in Ostia, Italy?
test.why: The floor in Ostia shows seven pictures, one for each step.

test.q: Which tool is shaped like a letter L?
test.why: A builder's square is shaped like an L. It makes straight corners.

test.q: Why do club members wear the same pin?
test.why: Badges and pins show which group you belong to.

choices: It swaps letters for shapes or numbers
test.why: A code swaps letters for shapes, numbers or other signs.

test.q: In the pigpen code, what does the middle letter E look like?
test.why: E sits in the middle of the grid, so lines go all around it. It is a full box.

test.q: Why could Leo not read his sisters' note?
choices: He did not have the key
test.why: A key shows which sign goes with which letter. Leo had no key.

test.q: Which secret is a happy surprise?
choices: A secret that makes you scared
test.why: A birthday card is a surprise. It is a happy secret that will be shared soon.

test.q: A secret is about someone getting hurt. What do you do?
test.why: An unsafe secret is always told to a trusted grown-up. Telling is brave.

write.prompt: Think about codes and passwords. Are they a good thing for a club to have? Tell or write your answer. Use two things you learned, like the pigpen code, the builders' password or safe secrets.
tips: Tell one thing from the unit, like the pigpen key.
Tell a second thing, like the fort password.
Say what makes a secret happy or unsafe.

title: Signs, Symbols and Secret Codes

chapters.title: Pictures That Talk
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a picture tell us something without any words?

story.title: The Picture on the Old Building
story.kicker: Maya sees a carved picture high on an old building. What is it trying to say?
paragraphs: Maya walks downtown with her grandpa. The buildings are tall and old. Maya looks up. High on one stone wall, she sees a carved picture. It has two tools that cross.
One tool looks like a big letter L. The other tool has two long legs, like an upside-down V. Maya pulls Grandpa's sleeve. "What does that picture mean?" she asks.
Grandpa smiles. "That is a symbol," he says. "It stands for builders. A club of people called Freemasons uses it. They met in this building long ago."
Maya looks again. The picture has no words. But now it tells her something. "Pictures can talk!" she says. Grandpa laughs. "Yes. You just have to learn how to listen."
story.think: Have you seen a picture on a wall or a sign that made you wonder what it meant? What did you think it said?

lessons.title: A Picture Means an Idea
lessons.mainIdea: A symbol is a picture that stands for an idea.
reading: Sam draws a red heart on a card for his mom. The heart does not say any words. But Mom knows what it means. It means "I love you."
A *symbol* is a picture that stands for an idea. A heart stands for love. A smiley face stands for happy. A star can stand for a great job.
You see symbols every day. You see them on doors, on boxes, and on screens. When you know the idea, you can read the picture.

words.d: a picture or shape that stands for an idea

look.title: Three Pictures on a Card
look.text: Look at the card on the table. In one corner is a red heart. In the middle is a big yellow smiley face. At the bottom is a gold star.
look.prompt: Say what each picture means. Which one would you put on a card for a friend?

check.q: What is a symbol?
choices: A picture that stands for an idea
A long word with many letters
A sound that a dog makes
check.why: The reading says a symbol is a picture that stands for an idea.

check.q: What does the red heart on Sam's card mean?
check.why: Sam's mom knows the heart means "I love you."

check.q: What can a star stand for?
check.why: The reading says a star can stand for a great job.

lessons.title: Signs on the Road
lessons.mainIdea: Road signs use shapes and colors so people can read them fast.
reading: Lee rides in the car with his dad. They come to a red sign with eight sides. Dad stops the car. The sign did not need to say a lot. Its shape and color told Dad what to do.
A *sign* is a board that gives a message. A stop sign is red. It has eight sides. No other road sign has that shape. So drivers know it fast, even from far away.
A yield sign has three sides. It means slow down and let others go first. A school sign has five sides. It means children may be near.

words.d: a board with a picture, shape or words that gives a message

look.title: How Many Sides?
look.cite: Federal Highway Administration, Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, 2009 edition
look.prompt: Which sign has the most sides? Draw that shape in the air with your finger.

check.q: How many sides does a stop sign have?
check.why: A stop sign is red and has eight sides.

check.q: What does a yield sign tell a driver?
choices: Slow down and let others go first
check.why: The reading says a yield sign means slow down and let others go first.

check.q: Why can drivers know a stop sign fast?
choices: Its shape and color are special
check.why: The stop sign is red with eight sides. No other road sign has that shape.

lessons.title: A Floor With Seven Steps
lessons.mainIdea: Long ago, a group in Italy put seven pictures on a floor to show seven steps.
reading: Ostia is an old town in Italy, near the sea. Long ago, a group met there. That was more than 1,700 years ago. They put a picture floor in their hallway. It is made of tiny stones.
The floor has seven pictures in a row, like a *ladder*. Each picture is one step. New members started on the first step. They could climb higher over time.
The first step was called the Raven. A raven is a big black bird. The top step was called the Father. The floor shows the whole ladder with no words needed.

words.d: steps that go up, one after another
a picture made from many tiny pieces of stone or glass

look.title: The Floor at Ostia
look.text: A hallway floor in Ostia, Italy, is a mosaic in seven panels, one for each step of the group. Each panel has its own pictures and a planet. One more panel shows the name Felicissimus. Diggers found it in 1940.
look.cite: Mithraeum.eu, entry on the Mithraeum of Felicissimus, Ostia; Parco archeologico di Ostia antica, educational panel "Mitreo di Felicissimo"
look.prompt: How many steps does the floor show? Why might a group show its steps in pictures?

check.q: In which country is the old town of Ostia?
check.why: The reading says Ostia is an old town in Italy, near the sea.

check.q: How many pictures are in the ladder on the floor?
check.why: The floor has seven pictures in a row. Each one is a step.

check.q: What was the first step called?
check.why: The first step was the Raven. The top step was the Father.

lessons.title: The Builders' Two Tools
lessons.mainIdea: The square and compass are real builders' tools, and Freemasons use them as a symbol.
reading: Pat builds a birdhouse. She uses a *square* to make each corner just right. The square is shaped like a big letter L.
She uses a *compass* to draw a perfect circle for the door. A compass has two legs. One leg stays still. The other leg turns around it.
Long ago, stone builders used these same tools. A club called the Freemasons began with builders. Today Freemasons still use the square and compass as their symbol.

words.d: a builder's tool shaped like an L, used to make straight corners
a tool with two legs, used to draw circles

look.title: Two Tools That Cross
look.text: Look at the picture carved in the stone. An L-shaped square points down. A compass with two long legs points up. The two tools cross in the middle, like a diamond.
look.prompt: Which tool makes corners? Which tool draws circles? Show each shape with your hands.

check.q: What does a compass help you draw?
check.why: Pat uses a compass to draw a perfect circle.

check.q: What shape is a builder's square?
check.why: The reading says the square is shaped like a big letter L.

check.q: Which club uses the square and compass as its symbol?
check.why: Freemasons began with builders. They still use these tools as their symbol.

lessons.title: Reading Old Buildings
lessons.mainIdea: Carvings on old buildings can tell us who built or used them.
reading: Jin looks at his school door. Above it, carved in stone, is an open book. The book tells people that this is a place to learn.
Old buildings often have *carvings*. A carving is a picture cut into stone or wood. Some carvings show the group that built or used the building.
See a square and compass? Freemasons may have met there. You can be a symbol detective. Look up, look close, and ask what the picture says.

words.d: a picture cut into stone or wood

look.title: Look Up on Your Street
look.text: Picture a walk on your street. Look up above the doors. One door has a stone book. One has a bell. One has two crossing tools, a square and a compass.
look.prompt: Pick one carving. What could it tell you about the building?

check.q: What is a carving?
choices: A picture cut into stone or wood
check.why: The reading says a carving is a picture cut into stone or wood.

check.q: What does the open book over Jin's school door tell people?
choices: This is a place to learn
check.why: The book tells people the building is a place to learn.

check.q: What can a square and compass on a wall mean?
check.why: The reading says a square and compass can mean Freemasons met in the building.

lessons.title: Badges, Pins and Flags
lessons.mainIdea: Badges, pins and flags show which group you belong to.
reading: Rosa wears a small pin shaped like a leaf. Her friend has the same pin. They are both in the garden club. The pin shows they belong together.
A *badge* is a small sign you wear to show your group. Scouts wear badges. Team players wear the same colors. Long ago, many clubs had their own badges and pins.
A *flag* shows a group too. The flag of the United States has 50 stars and 13 stripes. Each star stands for one state. Illinois is one of those stars.

words.d: a small sign you wear to show a group you belong to
a piece of cloth with colors and pictures that stand for a group or place

look.title: Count the U.S. Flag
look.cite: United States Code, Title 4, Section 1 (the flag: 13 stripes, a star for each state)
look.prompt: Which number is the biggest? What does each star stand for?

check.q: Why do Rosa and her friend wear the same leaf pin?
choices: They are in the garden club
check.why: The pin shows they belong to the same garden club.

check.q: How many stars are on the flag of the United States?
check.why: The flag has 50 stars, one for each state. It has 13 stripes.

check.q: What is a badge?
choices: A small sign you wear to show your group
check.why: The reading says a badge is a small sign you wear to show your group.

lessons.title: Make a Class Symbol
lessons.mainIdea: A class can make its own symbol to show what it cares about.
reading: Room 12 wants a symbol. First, they talk. They love to read. They love to help. They ask, what picture could show both ideas?
Mia draws a book. Omar draws two hands. The class puts them together: two hands holding a book. Now they have a class symbol. It is their own *design*.
A good symbol is simple. It is easy to draw and easy to see. It shows an idea the group shares. Everyone can help make it.

words.d: a plan or drawing you make for something new

look.title: Plan Your Class Symbol
look.text: Step 1: Say one thing your class loves. Step 2: Think of a picture for it. Step 3: Draw it big and simple. Step 4: Share it and add a friend's idea.
look.prompt: What does your class love? Draw a simple picture that shows it.

check.q: What did Room 12 put together for its symbol?
check.why: Mia drew a book and Omar drew two hands. The class put them together.

check.q: What makes a good symbol?
choices: It is simple and easy to see
Only one person can draw it
check.why: The reading says a good symbol is simple, easy to draw and easy to see.

check.q: What did Room 12 do first?
choices: They talked about what they love
check.why: First, the class talked. They love to read and to help.

review.q: A picture that stands for an idea is called a what?
review.why: A symbol is a picture that stands for an idea, like a heart for love.

review.q: Which road sign has eight sides?
review.why: The stop sign is red and has eight sides.

review.q: What does the old floor in Ostia show?
review.why: The floor in Ostia shows seven pictures, one for each step of the group.

review.q: Which tool has two legs and draws circles?
review.why: A compass has two legs. One stays still and one turns to draw a circle.

review.q: What does a badge or pin show?
review.why: Badges and pins show which group you belong to, like Rosa's garden club pin.

review.q: Maya sees a square and compass on an old building. What can it tell her?
review.why: Grandpa says the square and compass stand for builders and the Freemasons, who met there.

chapters.title: Our Own Secret Code
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a code work, and when is a secret OK to keep?

story.title: Notes About the Cookies
story.kicker: Two sisters send notes in a secret code. Can you find the cookies?
paragraphs: Ana and Lucy are sisters. Grandma baked cookies for the family party. The sisters hid the cookie box as a surprise. Now they want to send notes about it.
Ana draws on a paper. She makes little boxes, corners and dots. It looks like a puzzle. Lucy gets out a card with a tic-tac-toe grid. That card is their key.
Lucy matches each shape to a letter. Slowly, a word appears: SHELF. She smiles. The cookies are on the top shelf! Their brother Leo cannot read the note. He does not have the key.
At the party, the sisters bring out the box. "Surprise!" they shout. Everyone gets a cookie. Mom laughs. "Your secret was a happy one," she says. "Those are the best kind."
story.think: Why could Lucy read the note but Leo could not? What made this a happy secret?

lessons.title: Swap Letters for Shapes
lessons.mainIdea: A code swaps letters for shapes or numbers.
reading: Ben writes his name as 2, 5, 14. Why? B is letter 2. E is letter 5. N is letter 14. He swapped each letter for a number.
A *code* is a way to swap letters for shapes, numbers or other signs. The message stays the same. It just looks different. Only some people can read it.
You can make a code with numbers, colors or little pictures. Each letter gets its own sign. Then you write your message with the signs.

words.d: a way to swap letters for shapes, numbers or other signs

look.title: A Number Name
look.text: Look at this note on the desk: 1, 14, 1. The code is A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, and so on. N is letter 14. So the note spells a short name.
look.prompt: Read the name in the note. Now write your own name with numbers.

check.q: What does a code do?
choices: It swaps letters for shapes or numbers
check.why: The reading says a code swaps letters for shapes, numbers or other signs.

check.q: In Ben's code, what number is the letter B?
check.why: B is the second letter, so Ben writes it as 2.

check.q: What name does the note 1, 14, 1 spell?
check.why: A is 1 and N is 14. So 1, 14, 1 spells ANA.

lessons.title: Every Code Needs a Key
lessons.mainIdea: A key shows which sign goes with which letter.
reading: Lucy has a card that shows each shape and its letter. With the card, she reads Ana's note. Leo has no card. To him, the note is just marks.
The card is called a *key*. A key tells you which sign goes with which letter. With the key, you can read a code. Without it, a code is very hard to read.
Keep your key safe. Share it only with the people you want to read your notes. That is how a code works in a game.

words.d: a list that shows which sign goes with which letter

look.title: Two Friends, One Key
look.text: Look at two friends at a table. Each one has the same small card. The card shows a star for A, a moon for B and a sun for C. A third friend has no card.
look.prompt: Which friends can read a note in star, moon and sun? How could the third friend join the game?

check.q: What does a key show?
choices: Which sign goes with which letter
check.why: The reading says a key tells you which sign goes with which letter.

check.q: Why could Leo not read the note?
check.why: Leo had no card. Without the key, the note is just marks.

check.q: Who should you share your key with?
choices: The people you want to read your notes
check.why: The reading says to share the key only with people you want to read your notes.

lessons.title: Letters in a Grid
lessons.mainIdea: The pigpen code puts letters in a tic-tac-toe grid and an X.
reading: Draw a tic-tac-toe grid. Put A, B and C in the top row. Put D, E and F in the middle. Put G, H and I on the bottom. Now each letter has its own little pen.
This is the *pigpen code*. Each letter is the lines around it. E sits in the middle, so E is a full box. A sits in a corner, so A is just a corner shape.
Two grids and two X shapes hold all 26 letters. Some letters get a dot. The dot tells them apart. The letters sit in pens. That is why we call it pigpen!

words.d: a code that writes each letter as the lines of a grid or X around it
lines that cross to make rows of boxes

look.title: Where the 26 Letters Go
look.cite: The common pigpen key; see Klaus Schmeh, "Ten Peculiar Uses of the Pigpen Cipher," 2016
look.prompt: How many letters go in the two grids? How many go in the two X shapes?

check.q: What shape is the pigpen letter E?
check.why: E sits in the middle of the grid. Lines are all around it, so it is a full box.

check.q: Why is it called the pigpen code?
choices: The letters sit in pens, like pigs
check.why: The letters sit in little pens made by the lines, like pigs in pens.

check.q: What helps tell some pigpen letters apart?
check.why: The reading says some letters get a dot to tell them apart.

lessons.title: Pigpen on Old Stones
lessons.mainIdea: Long ago, people carved pigpen letters on stones.
reading: In New York City, there is an old churchyard. It is called Trinity Churchyard. One stone there is from 1794. It has a line of little boxes, corners and dots.
Those marks are pigpen letters. They are *carved* into the stone. For a long time, people walked by and wondered what they said. Then people used the key and read it.
The stone also shows a square and compass. That tells us the man was a Freemason. Many Freemasons knew the pigpen code long ago.

words.d: cut into stone or wood
a member of an old club that began with stone builders

look.title: A Stone in New York
look.text: An old stone in Trinity Churchyard in New York City is for James Leeson, who died in 1794. It shows a square and compass. It also has a line in pigpen code. Anyone with the key can read it.
look.cite: Atlas Obscura, "Trinity Churchyard" (place entry on the James Leeson stone)
look.prompt: What two kinds of symbols are on the stone? How can a person read the pigpen line?

check.q: In which city is Trinity Churchyard?
check.why: The reading says the old churchyard is in New York City.

check.q: How old is the stone with pigpen letters?
check.why: The stone in Trinity Churchyard is from 1794.

check.q: What else is on the stone besides pigpen letters?
check.why: The stone shows a square and compass, the symbol of the Freemasons.

lessons.title: A Password Shows You Belong
lessons.mainIdea: A password is a secret word that shows you belong to a group.
reading: Kim knocks on the blanket fort. "Password?" asks her brother. "Pancakes!" says Kim. He lets her in. The word shows she is part of the fort club.
A *password* is a secret word that lets you in. Long ago, Scotland had stone builders. They had a secret word too. A builder used it to show he was trained.
Builders also had to remember their lessons. In 1599, a leader made a rule. Each new builder must be tested on his memory. A password is something you keep in your memory.

words.d: a secret word that lets you in or shows you belong
what your mind keeps so you can know it later

look.title: A Rule for Builders, 1599
look.text: In Scotland in 1599, a rule for stone builders said a leader must test every worker and every new learner on how well they remembered their craft.
look.cite: Second Schaw Statutes, 28 December 1599, as printed in The Square magazine
look.prompt: Why would builders want to test what a new worker remembered?

check.q: What was the password for the blanket fort?
check.why: Kim says "Pancakes!" and her brother lets her in.

check.q: What did a stone builder in old Scotland use a secret word for?
check.why: The reading says a builder used the secret word to show he was trained.

check.q: In 1599, what did a rule say new builders must be tested on?
check.why: The 1599 rule said each new builder must be tested on his memory.

lessons.title: Hand Signals
lessons.mainIdea: A hand signal is a sign with your hands that gives a message with no words.
reading: Coach Rivera taps her head. The team knows what it means: run to the base. She does not shout. She uses a *signal*.
A signal is a sign that gives a message. A hand signal uses your hands. A thumbs up can mean good. A raised hand in class can mean I want to talk.
Some clubs have their own handshake. Members know it, and it shows they belong. A handshake or signal is a quiet way to share a message.

words.d: a sign or move that gives a message without words

look.title: Our Quiet Signals
look.text: Picture your classroom. The teacher holds up two fingers. Hands go up for a question. A thumbs up means I am ready. A flat hand on the heart means I need a break.
look.prompt: Make up one hand signal for your class. What message will it give?

check.q: What is a signal?
choices: A sign or move that gives a message
check.why: The reading says a signal is a sign that gives a message.

check.q: What did Coach Rivera's tap on her head mean?
check.why: The team knows her tap means run to the base.

check.q: What can a club's handshake show?
choices: That it is time for lunch
check.why: The reading says a club handshake shows members belong.

lessons.title: Happy Secrets and Unsafe Secrets
lessons.mainIdea: A happy secret is a surprise. An unsafe secret is one you always tell.
reading: Ana and Lucy hid the cookies for a party. Soon everyone knew. That was a *surprise*. A surprise is a happy secret that will be shared soon.
Some secrets are not happy. A secret about someone getting hurt is *unsafe*. A secret about touching or danger is unsafe. So is a secret that makes you feel scared.
Codes and passwords are for fun and games. They are never for hiding something unsafe. You never have to keep an unsafe secret.

words.d: a happy secret that will be shared soon
could hurt someone or put someone in danger

look.title: Sort the Secrets
look.text: Secret 1: We made a birthday card for Dad. Secret 2: Someone said, do not tell that I pushed you. Secret 3: The class password is Pancakes.
look.prompt: Which secrets are happy? Which one is unsafe and must be told to a grown-up?

check.q: What is a surprise?
choices: A secret about someone getting hurt
A secret that makes you scared
A happy secret that will be shared soon
check.why: The reading says a surprise is a happy secret that will be shared soon.

check.q: Which secret is unsafe?
choices: A secret about someone getting hurt
check.why: A secret about someone getting hurt is unsafe. You always tell it.

check.q: What are codes and passwords for?
check.why: The reading says codes and passwords are for fun and games, never for hiding something unsafe.

lessons.title: Tell a Trusted Grown-Up
lessons.mainIdea: If a secret is unsafe, tell a trusted grown-up right away.
reading: Tomas has a secret that makes his tummy feel tight. He goes to his teacher, Ms. Park. He tells her. She listens. She thanks him and helps.
A *trusted grown-up* is an adult who keeps you safe. It can be a parent, a teacher, a school nurse or a counselor. You can tell them anything.
Telling is brave. It is not tattling. If the first grown-up does not help, tell another one. Keep telling until someone helps.

words.d: an adult who listens to you and helps keep you safe

look.title: My Helping Hand
look.text: Trace your hand on paper. On each finger, write or draw one trusted grown-up. One finger could be a parent. One could be a teacher. One could be the school nurse.
look.prompt: Who are five grown-ups you could tell if a secret felt unsafe?

check.q: Who did Tomas tell his secret to?
check.why: Tomas went to his teacher, Ms. Park, and told her.

check.q: What should you do if the first grown-up does not help?
check.why: The reading says to keep telling until someone helps.

check.q: Is telling an unsafe secret tattling?
check.why: The reading says telling is brave. It is not tattling.

review.q: What do you need to read a code?
review.why: A key shows which sign goes with which letter. Without it, a code is hard to read.

review.q: The pigpen code puts letters in what shapes?
choices: A tic-tac-toe grid and an X
review.why: Pigpen puts the letters in two grids and two X shapes.

review.q: Where is an old stone with pigpen letters from 1794?
review.why: The stone in Trinity Churchyard, New York City, is from 1794.

choices: A secret word that shows you belong
review.why: A password is a secret word that lets you in, like Kim's fort password.

review.q: Ana and Lucy hid cookies for a party. What kind of secret was it?
review.why: It was a surprise. Everyone got a cookie at the party.

review.q: A secret makes you feel scared. What should you do?
review.why: An unsafe secret is always told to a trusted grown-up.
